title: Erdős #606: Why the Forbidden Line Counts Are Exactly C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3
description: The arithmetic core of the Erdős–Salamon gap structure: the two unreachable distinct-line counts are exactly the Frobenius gaps {1,3} of the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩, where 2 and 5 are the line-count deficits of a collinear triple and quadruple.

meta.author: Erdős–Salamon (1988); formalization: Lean Genius Researcher
meta.assumptions: Fully machine-checked, 0 sorries, 0 axiom declarations; all theorems depend only on the foundational axioms propext / Classical.choice / Quot.sound (no sorryAx, no Lean.ofReduceBool — kernel-verified). Honest scope: this file proves the NUMBER-THEORETIC core that explains why the Erdős–Salamon forbidden set is exactly {C(n,2)−1, C(n,2)−3}, namely that the gap set of the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩ is exactly {1,3}. It does NOT prove geometric realizability (that disjoint collinear triples/quadruples can be embedded in the plane — the geometric content carried by the parent file's axioms), nor the open Erdős–Salamon threshold N₀ (OQ-01's literal question).
originalContributions: Identifies the Erdős–Salamon forbidden values {C(n,2)−1, C(n,2)−3} with the Frobenius gaps of the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩
frobenius_two_five: 3 is the Frobenius number of ⟨2,5⟩ (largest non-representable)
lineDeficit k = C(k,2)−1, with deficits 2 (triple) and 5 (quadruple) as the semigroup generators
forbidden_line_counts: in the deficit model the only unreachable counts at the top of [.,C(n,2)] are C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3

overview.historicalContext: Erdős Problem #606 asks which distinct-line counts are achievable by n points in the plane. Erdős and Salamon (1988) proved that, for all sufficiently large n, the achievable counts are exactly {1} ∪ ([n, C(n,2)] \ {C(n,2)−1, C(n,2)−3}) — every value in the top range except two specific gaps. The parent gallery entry (Erdos606Problem.lean) axiomatizes this characterization and explains the gap structure in prose, but does not formalize the underlying arithmetic. The exact threshold N₀ beyond which the characterization holds (OQ-01) remains a hard open question about small-n geometry.
overview.problemStatement: Why are the forbidden line counts exactly C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3, and no others? Placing k of the points on a common line collapses their C(k,2) pairs to a single line, dropping the line count by the deficit C(k,2)−1: 0 for an ordinary 2-point line, 2 for a triple, 5 for a quadruple. Using disjoint such groups, every achievable total deficit is a non-negative combination of these deficits — in particular of 2 (triples) and 5 (quadruples). Which deficits, hence which top-range line counts, are unreachable?
overview.proofStrategy: Reduce the gap structure to the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩ = {2a + 5b : a,b ∈ ℕ}. The headline lemma representable_iff shows by an elementary parity argument (omega) that n is representable iff n ∉ {1,3}; gaps_eq packages this as a set equality, and frobenius_two_five identifies 3 = 2·5 − 2 − 5 as the Frobenius number. The geometric link is lineDeficit k = k(k−1)/2 − 1, with lineDeficit 3 = 2 and lineDeficit 4 = 5 (both by decide), so triples and quadruples alone realize every representable deficit (representable_via_triples_quadruples). Translating deficits d back to line counts C(n,2) − d, forbidden_line_counts shows that for n ≥ 4 the only unreachable top-range counts are C(n,2)−1 (deficit 1) and C(n,2)−3 (deficit 3), while C(n,2), C(n,2)−2, C(n,2)−4 are reachable.
keyInsights: The two Erdős–Salamon gaps are not an accident of the geometry but a shadow of a classical number-theoretic fact: the numerical semigroup generated by 2 and 5 has Frobenius number 3 and gap set exactly {1, 3}.

The generators 2 and 5 are the smallest positive line-count deficits: a collinear triple (C(3,2)−1 = 2) and a collinear quadruple (C(4,2)−1 = 5). Every other deficit is built from these, so triples and quadruples alone suffice to realize every non-forbidden value.

Deficit 1 is impossible because a single rich line already removes at least 2 lines (3 pairs → 1 line); deficit 3 is impossible because 3 is not a non-negative combination of 2 and 5. These are precisely the C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3 gaps.

This file is purely the arithmetic core: it does not claim the geometric realizability of the configurations (that disjoint triples/quadruples embed in the plane), which is the genuine geometric content axiomatized in the parent, nor does it resolve the open threshold N₀.

conclusion.summary: The Erdős–Salamon forbidden line counts C(n,2)−1 and C(n,2)−3 are identified, with a fully verified 0-axiom Lean proof, as the Frobenius gaps {1,3} of the numerical semigroup ⟨2,5⟩, whose generators are the line-count deficits of a collinear triple (2) and quadruple (5). This formalizes the arithmetic the parent entry only described in prose.
conclusion.implications: Casting the gap structure as a numerical-semigroup phenomenon makes the count of forbidden values (exactly two) transparent and explains their specific positions, and suggests the analogous question in higher dimensions reduces to the gap structure of the semigroup generated by the hyperplane deficits C(k,d)−1.
openQuestions: What is the exact Erdős–Salamon threshold N₀ beyond which the characterization {1} ∪ ([n, C(n,2)] \ {C(n,2)−1, C(n,2)−3}) holds? (The literal OQ-01, unresolved here.)
Can the geometric realizability — that disjoint collinear triples and quadruples can be placed to realize each representable deficit — be formalized, removing the parent file's achievability axioms?
For points in ℝ^d, does the hyperplane-count gap set equal the gap set of the numerical semigroup generated by the deficits C(k,d)−1 for k ≥ d?
